official_skills.notes: Uses the agentskillsforall CLI, not the skills CLI.

The repository README states it is a skill SOURCE repository, not installed directly; distribution happens through per-client plugins. Confirm the current install route before recommending a command. There is no per-SDK repository such as sentry-nestjs-sdk.

gap_map.why_it_matters: No NestJS-team skill collection was found on 2026-08-27. Community collections exist but none is canonical, so recommending one would push a stranger's opinions into every future decision on the project.
gap_map.fallback: The mentor works from the codebase and from NestJS documentation on demand, and states plainly that no framework-team skill is available for this stack.

gap_map.why_it_matters: Nest's DI container makes it trivial to mock everything, which produces suites that pass while the wiring is broken. Someone has to decide which seams are real and which mocks are lies.
gap_map.fallback: The mentor applies references/quality-gate.md, and requires at least one test per feature that exercises the real module wiring.

gap_map.why_it_matters: Guards and interceptors are easy to add and easy to forget. An endpoint with no guard looks identical to one that is intentionally public.
gap_map.fallback: The mentor requires every new controller route to declare its authorization decision explicitly, including 'public on purpose'.

layers.name: unit (isolated)
layers.belongs_here: a provider instantiated manually with its dependencies passed in - pure business rules
layers.cost: cheapest; the Nest docs call this isolated testing
layers.signal_you_picked_wrong: the test builds a TestingModule to reach one pure function

layers.name: unit (TestingModule)
layers.belongs_here: a provider resolved through Test.createTestingModule with dependencies overridden
layers.cost: moderate; bootstraps a module the way main.ts does
layers.signal_you_picked_wrong: everything is overridden, so the test asserts the overrides

layers.name: e2e
layers.belongs_here: the interaction of classes and modules at an aggregate level, close to what an end user does - the Nest docs' own framing

testing.proportions: No proportions stated. The Nest docs do state the trigger for e2e: as the application grows it becomes hard to manually test the behaviour of every endpoint.
rules: At least one test per feature exercises the real module wiring. A suite where every dependency is overridden passes while the DI graph is broken.
Override with overrideProvider using useValue for a fake, useClass for a substitute implementation.
Globally registered guards, interceptors and filters must be registered with useExisting to be overridable in a test.
Request-scoped providers are garbage-collected after the request; use ContextIdFactory to reach them in a test rather than asserting on a stale instance.
Nest is agnostic about the test runner. Read package.json instead of assuming Jest.
traps: The DI container makes it trivial to mock everything, which produces suites that pass while the wiring is broken - the single most common failure in this stack.
A globally registered enhancer registered with useClass cannot be overridden, so the test silently runs against the real one.
Request-scoped providers: the instance the test holds is not the instance the request used.
An e2e test sharing a database with another e2e test passes alone and fails in the suite, or worse, the reverse.
Validation pipes applied globally in main.ts but not in the testing module mean e2e tests accept payloads production rejects.
what_not_to_test: That a provider is defined - a test asserting only toBeDefined() proves the container started.
Framework behaviour: that a guard runs, that a pipe validates a decorated DTO.
DTO classes with no logic beyond decorators.
testing.notes: The Nest CLI scaffolds test, test:e2e and test:cov scripts. Read package.json before assuming they exist - projects rename them.

growth_thresholds.extract_shared_module: >=2 feature modules import the same provider
growth_thresholds.split_module: a module declares more than 10 providers

architecture.pattern: feature modules over a DI container

layers.name: Controller
layers.holds: HTTP transport: routing, request shape, response shape
layers.must_not: business rules - a controller method past about 30 lines has absorbed the service

layers.name: Service / Provider
layers.holds: the business rules, injectable and testable without HTTP
layers.must_not: knowledge of the request, the response or any Nest decorator beyond @Injectable

layers.name: Repository / data access
layers.must_not: business rules; it returns data, it does not decide policy

layers.name: Module
layers.holds: the wiring: what a feature provides, imports and exports

layers.name: Guards, interceptors, pipes, filters
layers.holds: cross-cutting concerns applied by decorator or globally
layers.must_not: feature-specific branching hidden from the feature that depends on it

variants.name: Feature modules in one app
variants.use_when: the default for a single deployable
variants.cost: module boundaries are conventions; nothing stops a cross-feature import but review

variants.name: Monorepo with libraries
variants.use_when: >=2 apps share the same providers, or teams own separate areas
variants.cost: build and release complexity you now maintain

variants.name: Hexagonal / ports and adapters
variants.use_when: the domain must outlive the framework, or persistence will be swapped
variants.cost: an interface and an adapter for every boundary - the over-abstraction signal unless a second adapter is real

rules: A controller translates HTTP and delegates. Business rules live in a provider that can be tested without an HTTP request.
A feature module exports only what other modules legitimately need. Everything else stays private to the module.
Every new route states its authorization decision explicitly, including 'public on purpose'. An unguarded route and an intentionally public one look identical in the code.
Register globally-applied enhancers with useExisting rather than useClass, or they cannot be overridden in tests.
Never inject a request-scoped provider into a singleton: it silently promotes the whole chain to request scope.
architecture.component_library: Not applicable - promote shared providers into a module that both features import, at >=2 consumers.
architecture.notes: Nest is unopinionated about folder layout but strongly opinionated about the DI graph. The module boundary, not the folder, is the real architecture.

key_decisions.why_it_is_forced: Nest bundles no persistence layer and integrates with several equally supported options.
key_decisions.reasonable_default: Prisma or Drizzle for a new project; whatever the team already runs otherwise.
key_decisions.cost_of_getting_it_wrong: It reaches every repository and every test fixture. Swapping it later is a rewrite of the data layer.

key_decisions.why_it_is_forced: Guards are a mechanism, not a policy. Nest gives you the hook and no decision.
key_decisions.reasonable_default: Decide the mechanism once, and make the per-route decision explicit for every route.
key_decisions.cost_of_getting_it_wrong: Authorization added feature by feature ends up enforced in some routes and forgotten in others, and nothing surfaces the gap.

key_decisions.why_it_is_forced: A global ValidationPipe and per-route pipes both work, and they behave differently in tests.
key_decisions.reasonable_default: A global pipe, replicated in the testing module so e2e tests reject what production rejects.
key_decisions.cost_of_getting_it_wrong: A mismatch means tests accept payloads the deployed app refuses, so the bug ships.

key_decisions.why_it_is_forced: Nest ships ConfigModule but takes no position on where values come from or how they are validated.
key_decisions.reasonable_default: Validate configuration at startup and fail loudly. A missing variable should stop the boot, not surface as a null at 3am.
key_decisions.cost_of_getting_it_wrong: Config read lazily fails in production on the one path nobody exercised.

key_decisions.why_it_is_forced: A monolith, a monorepo of apps and microservices are all first-class in Nest, and the transport choice is structural.
key_decisions.reasonable_default: Single app until an actual scaling or ownership boundary appears.
key_decisions.cost_of_getting_it_wrong: Splitting into services early buys distributed-systems problems before you have the problem they solve.

operability.observability: Nest ships a Logger with a replaceable implementation, and an exception filter is the single place an unhandled error can be captured before it becomes a 500 with no record.
operability.authorization: Guards. A globally registered guard is invisible at the call site, so the strategy must be written down or a reader cannot tell a public route from an unguarded one.
done_checks: clean install from a fresh clone
rules: Every controller route states its authorization decision, including 'public on purpose'.
Every outbound call states a timeout and a retry count including zero.
An exception filter reports unhandled errors somewhere a human sees them. Without it a 500 leaves no trace.
Configuration is validated at boot. A missing variable should fail the deploy, not the first request.
Nothing request-scoped is stored on a singleton provider.

dead_code_risks: Providers resolved by injection token or by string, never imported by class
Guards, interceptors, pipes and filters applied via decorators or APP_GUARD-style global providers
DTO classes referenced only through decorator metadata
Entities discovered by an ORM glob pattern rather than by import
Controllers whose only inbound reference is the HTTP router
